text:
Recent work supports testing candidate discrimination before attributing weak rankings to embedding collapse; it does not establish the cause of Electronics performance. [gSASRec (2024)](https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2024/0939.pdf) identifies overconfidence from negative sampling and proposes calibrated gBCE, recommending 128–256 negatives and calibration t=0.75. [Scaled cross-entropy (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.14238) finds that loss choice can substantially strengthen traditional sequential recommenders; when full softmax is impractical, scaling the sampled normalization term is an effective alternative.

Harder negatives require care. [R²NS (WWW 2026)](https://renzhaochun.github.io/assets/pdf/WWW_2026_Camera_Ready.pdf) reports early training failures from introducing hard negatives too soon, motivating uniform warm-up followed by efficient candidate recall and curriculum sampling. [RoDPO (2026 preprint)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.29259), in multimodal sequential recommendation, reports better ranking with stochastic sampling from dynamic top-K pools than deterministic hardest-negative selection, attributing gains partly to reduced false-negative suppression. Transfer to ID-only SASRec remains unverified.

Compute matters alongside hardness: [CCE− (2025, revised 2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.09682) reports up to 2× faster training and over 10× lower memory for sampled CE, with benefits from balancing negative count and batch size. Practical inference: compare multi-negative sampled softmax and calibrated gBCE first; then test a uniform/stochastic-hard mixture after warm-up, excluding observed training positives. Select by pinned macro validation HR@10 at matched GPU time, report Electronics separately, and track throughput and rank changes. Larger training margins alone cannot establish ranking gains or diagnose collapse.
